author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This function counts how many **subarrays** of `arr` have an **odd sum**, using the trick that a subarray's sum is just the difference of two **prefix sums**, and that difference is odd only when one prefix sum is even and the other is odd. As it walks through the array it keeps a running `prefixSum` plus two tallies: `evenCount` (how many earlier prefix sums were even, starting at `1` for the empty prefix) and `oddCount` (how many were odd). Whenever the current `prefixSum` is **even**, every earlier **odd** prefix pairs with it to form an odd-sum subarray, so it adds `oddCount` to `count` and bumps `evenCount`; when it is **odd**, it adds `evenCount` and bumps `oddCount`. The running `count` is reduced modulo `10^9 + 7` each step to avoid overflow, and the final total is returned after a single **O(n)** pass.

aiExplanation: This is the **brute-force** approach to counting subarrays with an odd sum: the outer loop picks every possible starting index `i`, and the inner loop extends the subarray one element at a time to each ending index `j`, keeping a running `sum` so each extension costs only one addition. After every extension it checks `sum & 1`, a **bitwise test** that is truthy exactly when the sum is odd, and if so increments `odd` while keeping it under `10^9 + 7` with the modulo. Because it examines all **O(n²)** start/end pairs explicitly, it is simple to reason about but far too slow for large inputs, which is why it times out on LeetCode.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This solution counts odd-sum subarrays in one **O(n)** pass by tracking, for each position, how many subarrays **ending at that element** have an odd sum (`odd`) and how many have an even sum (`even`). When the current `num` is **odd** (checked with the bitwise `num & 1`), appending it flips the parity of every subarray ending at the previous element, so the old `even` subarrays become odd and the old `odd` ones become even; the `+ 1` accounts for the new single-element subarray `[num]`, which is itself odd. That flip is done in one line with **array destructuring**: `[odd, even] = [even + 1, odd]`. When `num` is **even**, parities are unchanged and only the new single-element subarray is added, so `even++`. After each step it adds the current `odd` count to `res` (modulo `10^9 + 7`), and the accumulated total is the answer.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This is the same linear-time idea as the destructuring version, but it performs the swap with an explicit **temporary variable** instead of array destructuring, which avoids allocating a throwaway array on every odd element. The variables `odd` and `even` hold how many subarrays ending at the current position have an odd or even sum. When `num` is **odd** (`num & 1`), every previous subarray's parity flips, so the code saves the old `even` in `temp`, sets `even` to the old `odd`, and sets `odd` to `temp + 1`, where the extra `1` is the new one-element subarray containing just `num`. When `num` is **even**, nothing flips and only `even` grows by one. After each element it accumulates the current `odd` count into `res` modulo `10^9 + 7`, and that running total is returned as the number of odd-sum subarrays.
